key_points: Y-shaped airway stents treat central airway obstruction involving the lower trachea, main carina, and proximal mainstem bronchi.
Main indications include malignant stenosis (often from adjacent lung cancer) and select benign conditions (e.g., post-tracheostomy stenosis, tracheobronchomalacia) when surgery is not feasible.
Stent families: polymer (e.g., Dumon), hybrid (Dynamic), and self-expandable metallic; choice depends on airway biomechanics and lesion morphology.
Rigid bronchoscopy is preferred; metallic Y-stents are commonly deployed over two guidewires under fluoroscopy.
Frequent adverse events include mucostasis and granulation tissue; migration is uncommon with Y-stents due to their geometry.
Comparative data suggest higher insertion success and shorter implantation time with metallic Y-stents versus silicone, with similar early/late complications.

diagnostic_approaches: Define stenosis extent across distal trachea and main bronchi to size stent length.
Select stent diameter greater than the residual lumen after debulking/dilatation.
treatment_algorithms: Indications: malignant tracheobronchial stenosis (lung, esophageal, thyroid cancers, metastases); benign stenoses (post-tracheostomy, post-TB scar, amyloidosis, vasculitis, goiter); fistulas/dehiscences (tracheoesophageal, bronchopleural); select tracheobronchomalacia.
Benign disease: surgery remains the gold standard; use stents if inoperable or as a bridge.
Fistulas: consider combined esophageal + airway stenting; Dynamic Y-stent’s flexible posterior membrane can improve sealing against an esophageal stent.
Stent choice: polymer (Dumon/Hood), hybrid (Dynamic), self-expandable metallic; match to airway biomechanics and deployment constraints.
Comparison: in malignant main-carina disease, metallic Y-stents had fewer insertion failures and shorter implantation time than silicone, with no significant difference in early/late complications.

Implantation: general anesthesia and rigid bronchoscopy preferred; metallic Y-stents delivered under fluoroscopy over two guidewires; Dumon via pushing/pulling with dedicated rigid system; Dynamic via long-jaw forceps and pusher.
clinical_guidelines: No absolute contraindications in life-threatening main-carina obstruction; combine debulking (laser, APC, cryo) and dilatation as needed before stenting.
Size to cover both main bronchi and extend ≥5 mm into the trachea; diameter should exceed post-debulking lumen.
Monitor for mucostasis, granulation tissue, tumor overgrowth, and stent fracture; migration is rare with Y-stents.
Avoid permanent stenting for tracheobronchomalacia when possible due to long-term problems.

definitions.definition: Bifurcation airway stent with a tracheal body and two bronchial limbs used for lesions involving the main carina.
Silicone bifurcation stent with external studs to reduce migration and a smooth inner surface to limit incrustation.
Hybrid bifurcation stent with reinforced anterolateral wall and a flexible posterior membrane that mimics the pars membranacea.
Covered nitinol bifurcation stent deployed over guidewires under fluoroscopy; conforms to irregular airways.
Airway collapse due to cartilaginous destruction or membranous laxity; permanent stents are generally discouraged.
Abnormal connection between airway and esophagus; may require combined esophageal and airway stenting.

clinical_pearls: Choose stent length to cover both main bronchi and extend into trachea by ≥5 mm.
Dynamic Y-stent can seal fistulas better against an esophageal stent due to its flexible posterior membrane.
Saline inhalation and topical anti-inflammatory therapy help mitigate mucostasis.
Ensure smooth edges and proper sizing to reduce granulation tissue formation.
Stent migration is uncommon with Y-stents; reassess after tumor response or prolonged dilatation.
Adjunctive debulking and balloon dilatation before stent placement improve outcomes.

clinical_applications: Palliation of malignant central airway obstruction and sealing of tracheoesophageal/bronchopleural fistulas.
Bridge to tumor-specific therapy or surgery.
Temporizing option in inoperable benign stenoses or tracheobronchomalacia.
practice_recommendations: Use rigid bronchoscopy; plan sizing carefully; use fluoroscopy for metallic Y deployment.
Match stent type to airway biomechanics and fistula context (e.g., Dynamic with esophageal stent).
Schedule surveillance for mucostasis and granulation; debride as needed and consider adjunct therapies.
future_directions: Standardized complication reporting and time-to-event outcomes.
controversies: Optimal stent selection for mixed extrinsic compression and intraluminal disease.
Role of permanent stenting in benign tracheobronchomalacia.

points: Y-shaped stents restore patency across the main carina and may seal fistulas.
Material choice (polymer, hybrid, metallic) should reflect airway biomechanics and disease etiology.
Complications include mucostasis, granulation, tumor overgrowth, and fracture; careful sizing and follow-up mitigate risks.
